{{Short description|Whether a manifold which is a homotopy sphere is a sphere}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] area of [[topology]], the '''generalized Poincaré conjecture''' is a statement that a [[manifold]] that is a [[homotopy sphere]] {{em|is}} a [[n-sphere|sphere]]. More precisely, one fixes a [[category (mathematics)|category]] of manifolds: [[topological manifold|topological]] ('''Top'''), [[piecewise linear manifold|piecewise linear]] ('''PL'''), or [[differentiable manifold|differentiable]] ('''Diff'''). Then the statement is

:Every homotopy sphere (a closed ''n''-manifold which is [[Homotopy#Homotopy equivalence|homotopy equivalent]] to the ''n''-sphere) in the chosen category (i.e. topological manifolds, PL manifolds, or smooth manifolds) is isomorphic in the chosen category (i.e. [[homeomorphic]], PL-isomorphic, or [[Diffeomorphism|diffeomorphic]]) to the standard ''n''-sphere.

The name derives from the [[Poincaré conjecture]], which was made for (topological or PL) manifolds of dimension 3, where being a homotopy sphere is equivalent to being [[simply connected space|simply connected]] and [[closed manifold|closed]]. The generalized Poincaré conjecture is known to be true or false in a number of instances, due to the work of many distinguished topologists, including the [[Fields Medal]] awardees [[John Milnor]], [[Steve Smale]], [[Michael Freedman]], and [[Grigori Perelman]].

==Status==
Here is a summary of the status of the generalized Poincaré conjecture in various settings.

* '''Top''': True in all dimensions.
* '''PL''': True in dimensions other than 4; unknown in dimension 4, where it is equivalent to Diff.
* '''Diff''': False generally, with the first known counterexample in dimension 7 ([[Milnor sphere]]). True in some dimensions including 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 12, 56 and 61. This list includes all odd dimensions for which the conjecture is true. For even dimensions, it is true only for those on the list, possibly dimension 4, and possibly some additional dimensions <math>\ge 64</math> (though it is conjectured that there are none such).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang| first1=Guozhen |last2=Xu |first2=Zhouli |title=The triviality of the 61-stem in the stable homotopy groups of spheres| zbl=1376.55013 | journal=Ann. Math. |series=Second series| volume=186 | issue=2 |pages=501–580 | year=2017 | doi=10.4007/annals.2017.186.2.3 | arxiv=1601.02184}} See Corollaries 1.13 and 1.15 and Conjecture 1.17.</ref> The case of dimension 4 is equivalent to PL. 

Thus the veracity of the Poincaré conjectures is different in each category Top, PL, and Diff. In general, the notion of isomorphism differs among the categories, but it is the same in dimension 3 and below. In dimension 4, PL and Diff agree, but Top differs. In dimensions above 6 they all differ. In dimensions 5 and 6 every PL manifold admits an infinitely differentiable structure that is so-called ''Whitehead compatible''.<ref name="msp.warwick.ac.uk">See {{cite journal |url=https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/haupt/sandro.pdf |title=Fragments of Geometric Topology from the Sixties |first=Sandro |last=Buoncristiano |journal= Geometry & Topology Monographs |volume=6 |year=2003 }}</ref>

==History==
The cases ''n'' = 1 and 2 have long been known by the [[classification of manifolds]] in those dimensions.

For a PL or smooth homotopy n-sphere, in 1960 [[Stephen Smale]] proved for <math>n\ge 7</math> that it was homeomorphic to the ''n''-sphere and subsequently extended his proof to <math>n\ge 5</math>;<ref>{{cite journal |first=Stephen |last=Smale |title=Generalized Poincaré's conjecture in dimensions greater than four |journal=Ann. Math. |series=Second series |volume=74 |year=1961 |issue=2 |pages=391–406 |mr=0137124 |doi=10.2307/1970239 |jstor=1970239 }}</ref> he received a [[Fields Medal]] for his work in 1966.  Shortly after Smale's announcement of a proof, [[John R. Stallings|John Stallings]] gave a different proof for dimensions at least 7 that a PL homotopy ''n''-sphere was homeomorphic to the ''n''-sphere, using the notion of "engulfing".<ref>{{cite journal |first=John |last=Stallings |title=Polyhedral homotopy spheres |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=66 |year=1960 |issue=6 |pages=485–488 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1960-10511-3 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  [[Christopher Zeeman|E. C. Zeeman]] modified Stalling's construction to work in dimensions 5 and 6.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Erik Christopher |last=Zeeman |author-link=Christopher Zeeman |title=The Poincaré conjecture for ''n'' greater than or equal to 5 |journal=Topology of 3-manifolds and Related Topics (Proc. The Univ. Of Georgia Institute, 1961) |pages=198–204 |publisher=Prentice–Hall |location=Englewood Cliffs, NJ |year=1962 |mr=0140113 }}</ref>  In 1962, Smale proved that a PL homotopy ''n''-sphere is PL-isomorphic to the standard PL ''n''-sphere for ''n'' at least 5.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Stephen |last=Smale |title=On the structure of manifolds |journal=Amer. J. Math. |volume=84 |year=1962 |issue=3 |pages=387–399 |mr=0153022 |doi=10.2307/2372978 |jstor=2372978 }}</ref>  In 1966, [[Max Newman|M. H. A. Newman]] extended PL engulfing to the topological situation and proved that for <math>n \ge 5</math> a topological homotopy ''n''-sphere is homeomorphic to the ''n''-sphere.<ref>{{cite journal |author-link=Max Newman |first=M. H. A. |last=Newman |title=The Engulfing Theorem for Topological Manifolds |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |series=(2) |volume=84 |year=1966 |issue=3 |pages=555–571 |mr=0203708 |doi=10.2307/1970460 |jstor=1970460 }}</ref>

[[Michael Freedman]] solved the topological case <math>n = 4</math> in 1982 and received a Fields Medal in 1986.<ref>{{cite journal  |first=Michael |last=Freedman |author-link=Michael Freedman|title=The topology of four-dimensional manifolds |journal=[[Journal of Differential Geometry]] |volume=17 |year=1982 |issue=3 |pages=357–453 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214437136 |mr=0679066 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The initial proof consisted of a 50-page outline, with many details missing. Freedman gave a series of lectures at the time, convincing experts that the proof was correct. A project to produce a written version of the proof with background and all details filled in began in 2013, with Freedman's support. The project's output, edited by Stefan Behrens, Boldizsar Kalmar, Min Hoon Kim, Mark Powell, and Arunima Ray, with contributions from 20 mathematicians, was published in August 2021 in the form of a 496-page book, ''The Disc Embedding Theorem''.<ref name=quanta>{{cite news|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/new-math-book-rescues-landmark-topology-proof-20210909/|title=New Math Book Rescues Landmark Topology Proof|first=Kevin |last= Hartnett |publisher= Quanta Magazine|date=September 9, 2021}}</ref><ref>[https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-disc-embedding-theorem-9780198841319 The Disc Embedding Theorem]</ref>

[[Grigori Perelman]] solved the case <math>n = 3</math> (where the topological, PL, and differentiable cases all coincide) in 2003 in a sequence of three papers.<ref name="perelman200211">{{cite arXiv|last=Perelman|first=Grigori| author-link=Grigori Perelman|title=The entropy formula for the Ricci flow and its geometric applications|eprint = math.DG/0211159 | date = 11 November 2002}}</ref><ref name="perelman200303">{{cite arXiv|last=Perelman|first=Grigori|author-link=Grigori Perelman|title=Ricci flow with surgery on three-manifolds|eprint=math.DG/0303109 | date = 10 March 2003}}</ref><ref name="perelman200307">{{cite arXiv|last=Perelman|first=Grigori|author-link=Grigori Perelman|title=Finite extinction time for the solutions to the Ricci flow on certain three-manifolds|eprint=math.DG/0307245|date = 17 July 2003}}</ref> He was offered a Fields Medal in August 2006 and the [[Millennium Prize Problems|Millennium Prize]] from the [[Clay Mathematics Institute]] in March 2010, but declined both.

In the smooth category for <math> n>4</math>, studying the Poincaré conjecture comes down to determining the elements of the Kervaire-Milnor short [[exact sequence]] of groups

<math>0\to bP_{n+1} \to\Theta_{n}\to \pi_{n}^S/(\mathrm{Image}(J_{n}))\to 0\, </math>

where the order of the [[Kervaire–Milnor group]] <math>\Theta_{n}</math> equals the number of distinct smooth structures on <math> S^{n} \, (n>4)</math>. Here <math>\pi_{n}^S</math> is the <math> n</math>-th stable [[homotopy group]] and <math> J_n </math> is the [[J-homomorphism]] <math> J_{n} \colon \pi_{n}(\mathrm{SO}) \to \pi_{n}^S </math>, where <math>\mathrm{SO}</math>  is the infinite special [[orthogonal group]]. The [[quotient group]] <math> \pi_{n}^S/(\mathrm{Image}(J_{n})) </math> is usually denoted as <math>\mathrm{coker}(J_{n}) </math>, the [[cokernel]] of <math>J_{n}</math>. The remaining term in the short exact sequence, namely the group <math> bP_{n+1}</math>, denotes the <math>n</math>-dimensional homotopy spheres that bound an <math> n+1</math>-dimensional parallelizable manifold (note that in modern notation it has become customary to denote <math> bP_{n+1}</math> by the symbol <math> \Theta_{n}^{bp}</math>, instead). Importantly, <math> bP_{n+1}</math> has the additional property that it is trivial when <math> n</math> is even. Finally, the case where <math>n \equiv 2 \pmod{4}</math> has a slightly modified short exact sequence from the one given above, now involving the Kervaire invariant. Namely

<math>0\to bP_{4l+3} \to\Theta_{4k+2}\to \pi_{4k+2}^S/(\mathrm{Image}(J_{4k+2}))\xrightarrow{\Phi_{K}}\Z/2\to bP_{4k+2}\to 0\, </math>

where <math>\Phi_{K}</math> is the Kervaire invariant. When the Kervaire invariant is zero, i.e. when <math> n\ne 6, 14, 30, 62,</math> and <math>126 </math>, then this exact sequence reduces to the original exact sequence given above, but also gives the result that <math> bP_{4k+2}=\Z/2 </math>. Plugging this result into the original short exact sequence given above, this implies that <math> \Z/2 </math> is a subgroup of <math> \Theta_{4k+1}</math> and therefore <math> \Theta_{4k+1}</math> is nontrivial when the Kervaire invariant is zero for <math> n=4k+2</math>.

John Milnor solved the smooth case <math>n = 5</math> in 1959 in the unpublished manuscript "Differentiable Manifolds Which Are Homotopy Spheres." The results of this manuscript were later incorporated in a larger and later (1963) paper where the smooth cases <math>n = 6</math> and <math>n = 12</math> were also solved.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kervaire| first1=Michel |last2=Milnor |first2=John |title=Groups of Homotopy Spheres I|  journal=Ann. Math. |series=Second series| volume=186 | issue=2 |pages=504–537 | year=1963 }} </ref> The <math>n = 5</math> and <math>n = 6</math> cases also follow from Smale's PL result, since the smooth and PL categories coincide for <math>n \le 6</math>.

Daniel Isaksen solved the smooth case <math>n = 56</math> in 2014. This followed from his calculation of the stable homotopy group in dimension 56 being of order 2 (See page 4 in section 1.4 and Charts 8.1 and 8.17 in Stable Stems (2019) by Daniel C. Isaksen)<ref>{{cite book |last1=Isaksen| first1=Daniel  | title = Stable Stems | publisher = American Mathematical Society | volume = 262, No 1269| issn =0065-9266 |doi=10.1090/memo/1269 |series = Memoirs of the AMS|year =2019}}</ref>. Since the image of the J-Homomorphism in the Kervaire-Milnor short exact sequence is also of order 2, this shows that the cokernel of the J-homomorphism is trival. Since <math> bP_{57}</math> is trivial (since <math> bP_{2n+1}</math> is always trivial), <math> \Theta_{56}</math> is therefore trivial. Consequently, the number of smooth structures on <math> S^{56} </math> is one. Also, see Theorem 3.1.14 of Zhouli Xu's 2017 PhD thesis "In And Around Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres." See also section 2 in the review article Stable Homotopy Groups Of Spheres and Motivic Homotopy Theory (2023) by Daniel C. Isaksen, Guozhen Wang, and Zhouli Xu.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Isaksen| first1=Daniel |last2=Wang| first2=Guozhen|last3=Xu| first3=Zhouli | chapter = Stable Homotopy Groups Of Spheres and Motivic Homotopy Theory |pages = 2768-2790 |title = International Congress of Mathematicians 2022 July 6-14 | publisher = EMS Press | volume = IV |doi=10.4171/ICM2022/32 |editor-last1 = Beliaev| editor-first1 = Dmitry|editor-last2 = Smirnov| editor-first2 = Stanislav|year =2023}}</ref>

Guozhen Wang and Zhouli Xu solved the smooth case <math>n = 61</math> in 2017.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang| first1=Guozhen |last2=Xu |first2=Zhouli |title=The triviality of the 61-stem in the stable homotopy groups of spheres| zbl=1376.55013 | journal=Ann. Math. |series=Second series| volume=186 | issue=2 |pages=501–580 | year=2017 | doi=10.4007/annals.2017.186.2.3 | arxiv=1601.02184}} </ref>

It was known from a theorem of Kervaire and Milnor (see  Groups of Homotopy Spheres I (1963)) that the smooth Poincaré conjecture is always false for dimensions <math> n=4k+3 \,(k\ge 1) </math>. For dimensions <math> n=4k+1 \, (k\ge 1)</math> the answer depends on the existence of Kervaire invariant elements. Due to work of Hill, Hopkins and Ravenel<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hill| first1=M. A. |last2=Hopkins| first2=M. J.|author-link2=Michael J. Hopkins|last3=Ravenel| first3=D. C.|author-link3=Douglas Ravenel | title = On the nonexistence of elements of Kervaire invariant one| journal = Annals of Mathematics| volume = 184| pages = 1-262| doi = 10.4007/annals.2016.184.1.1 | year =2016}}</ref>, it was thus known that the only odd dimensions where the smooth Poincaré conjecture could be true were in dimensions 1, 3, 5, 13, 29, 61, and 125. [[J. Peter May]] ruled out the case of <math> n=13 </math><ref>{{cite book | type = PhD thesis |last1=May| first1=J. Peter | title = The Cohomology of Restricted Lie Algebras and of Hopf Algebras: Application to the Steenrod Algebra | year = 1964}}</ref>. The case <math>  n=29 </math>  was ruled out in the late 1960's by filling in the terms in the Kervaire-Milnor short exact sequence
<math>0\to bP_{30} \to\Theta_{29}\to \pi_{29}^S/(\mathrm{Image}(J_{29}))\to 0\, </math>.  J. Peter May showed in his PhD thesis that the only odd prime primary term in <math> \pi_{29}^S </math>, namely <math> p=3 </math>, is equal to <math> \mathbb{Z}_{3} </math>. Mark Mahowald and Martin Tangora then showed that the 2-primary term was trivial.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mahowald| first1=Mark |last2=Tangora | first2=Martin | title = Some Differentials In The Adams Spectral Sequence| journal = Topology| volume = 6| pages = 349-369| doi = 10.1016/0040-9383(67)90023-7  | year =1967}}</ref> This established that the stable homotopy group in dimension 29 is of order 3. William Browder showed that <math>  bP_{30}=0 </math> by establishing the existence of a framed manifold of Kervaire invariant 1 in dimension 30.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Browder| first1=William  | title = The Kervaire invariant of framed manifolds and its generalization| journal = Annals of Mathematics| volume = 90| pages = 157-186| doi = 10.2307/1970686  | year =1969}}</ref> Because the image of the J-homomorphism in dimension <math> 29 </math>, i.e., <math> J_{29} \colon \pi_{29}(\mathrm{SO}) \to \pi_{29}^S </math>, is trivial (because <math> \pi_{29}(\mathrm{SO}) </math> is trivial), the conclusion is that <math> \Theta_{29}=\mathbb{Z}_{3}</math> and therefore there are three different smooth structures on <math>  S^{29} </math>. Daniel Isaksen developed a more efficient and machine checkable method, namely motivic homotopy theory, that allowed calculations beyond <math> n=60 </math>. The final case <math> n=125 </math> was finally ruled out by Guozhen Wang and Zhouli Xu by producing an explicit element of <math> \pi_{125}^S/(\mathrm{Image}(J_{125})) </math> whose non-triviality is detected by the spectrum of topological modular forms (See Proposition 1.12 of their  2017 paper, "The Triviality of the 61-Stem in the Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres"). Thus, it is now known that the only odd dimensions where the smooth Poincaré conjecture is true are 1, 3, 5, and 61.

The smooth case in even dimensions has been checked in all even dimensions through <math>n = 138 </math><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Behrens| first1=M. | last2=Hill| first2=M. | last3=Hopkins| first3=M.J. |last4=Mahowald| first4=M. | title = Detecting exotic spheres in low dimensions using \mathrm{coker} J| journal = J. London Math. Soc.| volume = 2| pages = 1-46| doi = 10.1112/jlms.12301  | year =2020| arxiv=1708.06854}}</ref>, with the exception of <math>n = 4 </math>. So far, the only even dimensions where the smooth Poincaré conjecture has been found to be true are in dimensions <math>n = 2, 6, 12 </math> and <math> 56 </math>. In the even case, <math>\Theta_{2n} = \pi_{2n}^S/(\mathrm{Image}(J_{2n}))</math> because <math> bP_{2n+1}=0</math> in the Kervaire-Milnor short exact sequence, unless the Kervaire invariant is nonzero, in which case <math>\Theta_{2n}</math> is a subgroup. Therefore determining all smooth structures on <math> S^{2n} \, (n>2)</math> involves determining the structure of <math>\mathrm{cokernel}(J_{2n})\equiv \pi_{2n}^S/(\mathrm{Image}(J_{2n}))</math>. Disproving the Poincaré conjecture then amounts to finding a single nontrivial element in <math>\mathrm{cokernel}(J_{2n})</math>, with the caveat that the analysis is more complicated in the five even dimensions above <math> n=4 </math> where the Kervaire invariant is nonzero. The strategy has been to find nontrivial elements in low dimensions that are <math>\nu</math>-periodic, that is, that reappear every <math>\nu</math> dimensions. So, if there is a nontrivial element in dimension <math> D </math>, then there are nontrivial elements in all dimensions <math> D+\nu k \, (k\ge0) </math>. In this way, many infinite sequences of dimensions can be ruled out.

==PL==
For [[piecewise linear manifold]]s, the Poincaré conjecture is true except possibly in dimension 4, where the answer is unknown, and equivalent to the smooth case.
In other words, every compact PL manifold of dimension not equal to 4 that is homotopy equivalent to a sphere is PL isomorphic to a sphere.<ref name="msp.warwick.ac.uk"/>
